questions.prompt: What does a Punnett square actually predict?
options: The exact traits every single offspring will have, guaranteed
The probability of different genotype and phenotype combinations offspring could have
Which parent's genes are stronger overall
The exact number of offspring a pair will produce
questions.explanation: A Punnett square lays out probabilities based on how alleles can combine — it tells you the odds (like 3:1) across many offspring, not a certainty for any one individual.
questions.misconception: Students often think a 3:1 ratio means 'the first 3 offspring will show the trait and the 4th won't,' or that the square guarantees each offspring's traits — when really each offspring is an independent random combination, just like flipping a coin doesn't guarantee exactly 1 heads out of every 2 flips.

questions.prompt: In pea plants, R (round seeds) is dominant and r (wrinkled seeds) is recessive. What phenotype does a plant with genotype Rr have?
options: A blend of round and wrinkled
questions.explanation: Because R is dominant, one copy of R is enough to produce the round phenotype, even though the plant still carries a hidden r allele it could pass on.
questions.misconception: A common misconception is that heterozygous traits automatically blend together (like mixing paint), but in classic dominant/recessive inheritance the dominant allele fully masks the recessive one — there's no in-between look.

questions.prompt: If you cross two heterozygous pea plants (Rr x Rr), what phenotype ratio should the Punnett square predict?
questions.explanation: The genotype ratio is 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr, but since both RR and Rr look round (R is dominant), that combines to a 3 round : 1 wrinkled phenotype ratio.
questions.misconception: Students frequently mix up the genotype ratio (1:2:1) with the phenotype ratio, forgetting that Rr individuals show the dominant round phenotype even though their genotype is different from RR.

questions.prompt: What determines which allele a parent passes on to an offspring for a given gene?
options: The parent consciously chooses which trait to pass on
Each parent randomly passes just one of their two alleles during reproduction
Only the mother's alleles get passed on
Both of a parent's alleles are always passed on together
questions.explanation: During the formation of sex cells, a parent's allele pairs separate so that only one allele per gene ends up in each egg or sperm; which one gets passed is random. This is exactly why a Punnett square lists each parent's two alleles just once across the top and side.
questions.misconception: A common misconception is that offspring receive both of a parent's alleles, or that inheritance is somehow directed — missing that allele pairs randomly separate before fertilization, which is what makes the four boxes of a Punnett square equally likely outcomes.
